opening: Java is both a programming language and a software platform. Students write source code in the Java language, the compiler translates that source into class files, and a Java Virtual Machine executes the instructions stored in those class files. Understanding this path makes IDE messages, package rules, and portability much less mysterious.

An IDE does not replace the JDK. It organizes files and calls the compiler, launcher, and debugger on the student's behalf. A dependable developer can use the IDE productively and can also explain what its Build and Run buttons are doing.
Input is the boundary between a Java program and the outside world. Scanner converts incoming characters into tokens, lines, and typed values such as integers, prices, or names.
Reliable input code chooses a token-based or line-based strategy, validates before conversion, consumes invalid input so the program can advance, and closes file resources that the program owns.

sections.title: JDK, JRE and JVM
paragraphs: The Java Development Kit, or JDK, is the toolkit used to develop Java software. It includes javac for compilation, java for launching programs, debugging and documentation tools, and the runtime components required by those tools.

The Java Virtual Machine, or JVM, is the abstract execution environment for class files. The standard library is the collection of reusable APIs—such as String, Scanner, List, Files, and Thread—that applications call instead of rebuilding common facilities.
sections.note: Select a JDK for the project, not merely an editor. Without a configured JDK, the IDE has no compiler or Java platform against which to check the program.

sections.title: Skeleton of a Java Program
paragraphs: A Java source file contains a class, the class contains methods, and a method contains statements. This small program uses the conventional main method as its entry point. Follow the matching numbers to connect each piece of code with its meaning.
sections.note: Java is case-sensitive: First and first are different names. Save this public class as First.java. String and System need no import because java.lang is imported automatically.

sections.title: Reading from the Keyboard with Scanner
paragraphs: System.in is Java's standard input stream, normally connected to the keyboard. Scanner reads from that stream and converts input text into values such as integers, decimals, or strings. The keyboard supplies the input; Scanner is the tool that reads it.

Import java.util.Scanner, create a Scanner with new Scanner(System.in), then call its reading methods. In the example below, two calls to nextInt() read two integers into x and y. The program adds them and prints the result.
sections.caption: Java source · ReadKeyboard.java — this introductory example assumes two valid integers.
sections.note: Scanner belongs to java.util, so it needs an import. System belongs to java.lang, which is imported automatically. Reuse one Scanner for System.in; closing it also closes standard input.

sections.title: The main method and program boundaries
paragraphs: For a conventional class-based application, the launcher looks for public static void main(String[] args). public makes the entry point accessible, static allows it to run before an application object exists, void means it does not return a value to the JVM, and args carries command-line arguments.

A successful process normally reports exit code 0. An uncaught exception prints a stack trace and usually ends the process with a non-zero status. Output, error messages, and exit status are all evidence that should be inspected after a run.
sections.caption: Command-line arguments let one compiled program receive different values at launch time.

sections.title: Project structure and packages
paragraphs: A package name is a qualified type namespace, while a source root is the directory above the package hierarchy. A class declared in package ca.school.app conventionally lives at ca/school/app beneath the source root. Compilation output mirrors that hierarchy beneath the output directory.

Keeping generated .class files outside src prevents source and build artifacts from being mixed. Share source files and project configuration when needed; do not treat out or bin directories as the authoritative program.
sections.code:
project/
├── src/
│   └── ca/school/app/HelloJava.java
└── out/
    └── ca/school/app/HelloJava.class
sections.caption: The package begins below src in source code and below out in compiled output.

sections.title: From character stream to typed value
paragraphs: System.in represents standard input. Wrapping it in Scanner adds parsing operations. nextInt(), nextDouble(), and nextBoolean() read and convert one token; next() returns one token as text; nextLine() returns the remainder of a line.
Whitespace is the default delimiter, so next() cannot read a full name containing spaces. nextLine() can because its unit of work is the line rather than the token.
sections.caption: Typed methods consume a token; the explicit nextLine() keeps the later line read in sync.

sections.title: Validation must also make progress
paragraphs: If the next token is not a valid integer, nextInt() throws InputMismatchException. Interactive programs can test with hasNextInt() before conversion.
The invalid token must then be consumed. Otherwise the scanner sees the same bad token repeatedly and the program appears to freeze.
sections.caption: Every validation loop needs both a condition and a way to advance the input.

sections.title: The newline trap
paragraphs: Methods such as nextInt() stop after the number and leave the line separator waiting. A following nextLine() therefore reads the empty remainder of that line.
Either consume the pending newline once or read each field with nextLine() and convert explicitly. The second approach often gives larger applications more control over error messages.
sections.note: Choose one input strategy for each interaction instead of alternating casually between token and line methods.

sections.title: Files and resource ownership
paragraphs: Scanner applies the same token model to files. A file-backed scanner owns an operating-system resource and belongs in try-with-resources.
Standard input is shared by the process. Closing a scanner wrapping System.in also closes System.in, so the application should decide which component owns that scanner.
sections.caption: try-with-resources closes the file on normal and exceptional exits.

sections.title: Match look-ahead to the consuming method
paragraphs: hasNext(), hasNextLine(), hasNextInt(), and hasNextDouble() inspect input without consuming it. The check should match the next read.
Checking hasNext() and then calling nextDouble() proves only that some token exists, not that it is a valid decimal. Typed look-ahead makes the intended conversion explicit.
sections.caption: Validation and consumption should ask the same question about the next token.

terms: The development kit containing Java tools and platform components.
The execution environment defined for Java class files.
JVM instructions stored in a class file.
Locations in which Java tools search for compiled types and resources.
IDE settings that identify what to launch and with which arguments and environment.
A unit of text separated by Scanner's delimiter.
The pattern that separates tokens; whitespace by default.
Testing with hasNext… without consuming the token.
review: What work is performed by javac, and what work is performed by java?
Why is a configured JDK required even when an IDE is installed?
What does platform independence guarantee, and what does it not guarantee?
Why can nextLine() return an empty string immediately after nextInt()?
What must a validation loop do after detecting an invalid token?
When should a Scanner be placed in try-with-resources?

opening: Object-oriented design organizes a program around objects that own state and provide behavior. Its purpose is not merely to place variables inside classes. A good object protects its own validity, exposes a small and meaningful public interface, and can be replaced by another implementation when both obey the same contract.

The central progression is class and object, then encapsulation, inheritance, abstraction, interfaces, and polymorphism. Each idea addresses a different design problem; using them together without understanding those problems often produces rigid class hierarchies.

sections.title: Classes establish valid objects
paragraphs: A class defines the structure and behavior shared by a category of objects; an object is one runtime instance created from that definition. Fields record state, methods provide behavior, and constructors establish the initial state. A constructor has the class name, has no return type, and runs when new creates the object.
Overloaded constructors provide several valid ways to create an object. They should delegate where practical so that validation and initialization are not duplicated.
sections.caption: Encapsulation means the object, not its caller, enforces the invariant.

sections.title: Data hiding, properties, and arrays of objects
paragraphs: Data hiding places representation behind the class interface. A getter without a public setter creates read-only access for callers; a setter without a getter creates write-only access; providing both creates read-write access. These are API patterns rather than a separate Java property syntax. Validation belongs in constructors and mutating methods so that every public path preserves the object's rules.

An array of a class type stores references, not embedded objects. Creating new Student[3] produces three null elements. Each Student must still be constructed and assigned before a method can be called through that array element.
sections.caption: The array groups references; each object has a separate identity and state.

sections.title: Inheritance represents specialization
paragraphs: Generalization identifies behavior shared by several types and places it in a common contract. Specialization defines a more specific subtype. In Java, extends expresses class specialization and implements connects a class to an interface contract. A subtype should be usable wherever its parent type is expected.

The super keyword selects superclass construction or behavior; this refers to the current object. Superclass construction happens before subclass construction. If the parent has no no-argument constructor, the child constructor must explicitly call an available super(...) constructor as its first statement.
sections.note: Use composition when one object merely uses or contains another. Use inheritance when the relationship expresses a stable is-a contract.

sections.title: Overloading and overriding solve different problems
paragraphs: Overloading gives several methods the same name but different parameter lists. The compiler chooses the overload from the declared argument types. Changing only the return type is not sufficient.

Overriding gives a subclass a new implementation of an inherited instance method. The method signature must match and access cannot become more restrictive. At runtime, Java dispatches an overridden method according to the actual object type. Static, private, and final methods do not participate in ordinary dynamic overriding.
sections.caption: The reference type controls what may be called; the runtime object controls which override runs.

sections.title: Abstract classes and interfaces define contracts
paragraphs: An abstract class can store shared state, provide concrete behavior, and declare abstract methods. It cannot be instantiated, but a variable of the abstract type may refer to an object of a concrete subclass. A subclass must implement all inherited abstract methods or remain abstract itself.

An interface describes a capability. Its ordinary abstract methods are public, and its fields are constants: public, static, and final. Modern interfaces may also contain default, static, and private methods. A class may implement several interfaces, which provides multiple inheritance of contracts without inheriting conflicting instance state.

An interface reference is also useful for callbacks: one object registers an implementation, then later invokes the interface method without depending on the implementation class. This separates the caller from the concrete receiver.
sections.caption: The abstract class shares the family model; the interface names a reusable capability.

sections.title: Packages and access boundaries
paragraphs: Packages create namespaces and establish an access boundary. public is visible everywhere; protected is visible in the package and to subclasses under Java's inheritance rules; package-private is visible only within the package; private is visible only within the declaring top-level class and its nested types.

Package names conventionally use a reversed domain, such as ca.school.registration. The package declaration, directory structure, imports, compiler output, and classpath must agree. Packages are therefore part of a program's architecture, not merely labels at the top of files.

sections.title: A package is tested across files
paragraphs: Package access cannot be understood from a single isolated class. A useful exercise places a public model class and a package-private factory in ca.school.model, then places Main in ca.school.app. Main may import and use the public model class, but it cannot import the package-private factory.

Compile the complete source tree into a separate output directory. If the package statement and directory hierarchy disagree, the compiler or launcher will report that the expected type cannot be found.
sections.code:
javac -d out src/ca/school/model/*.java src/ca/school/app/Main.java
java -cp out ca.school.app.Main
sections.caption: Compilation establishes the output package tree; launching uses the fully qualified class name.

terms: A condition that must remain true for every valid object.
Keeping representation private and controlling access through behavior.
The read and write operations a class deliberately exposes for state.
A shared parent contract identified from several related specialized types.
Runtime selection of an overridden instance method.
Viewing a subclass object through a parent or interface reference.
The behavior callers may rely on, independent of implementation.
review: Why is a public field weaker than a private field plus behavior?
What does an array of a class type contain immediately after creation?
When is composition preferable to inheritance?
Which decision is made at compile time: overload selection or override dispatch?
Why can an abstract-type reference be useful even though the abstract class cannot be instantiated?
How does an interface support a callback?

opening: A nested type communicates ownership. It says that a helper class belongs conceptually to another class or to one method. Java provides four forms—member inner, static nested, local, and anonymous—and the important difference is what context each form captures.

sections.title: Member inner classes carry an outer object
paragraphs: A non-static member inner class is associated with one enclosing instance. It can directly access private instance fields of that outer object. Construction therefore requires an outer instance first.
sections.code:
Outer outer = new Outer();
Outer.MemberInner inner = outer.new MemberInner();
sections.caption: The unusual construction syntax makes the hidden outer reference visible.

sections.title: Static nested classes do not capture an instance
paragraphs: A static nested class is namespaced inside its enclosing class but has no implicit outer object. It can directly use only static members unless a reference to an outer object is passed explicitly. Choose this form when nesting improves organization but instance capture is unnecessary.
sections.code: Outer.StaticNested helper = new Outer.StaticNested();
sections.caption: Static nested classes behave much like ordinary classes with a qualified name.

sections.title: Local and anonymous classes
paragraphs: A local class is declared inside a block, usually a method, and is visible only there. An anonymous class defines and instantiates a one-off subclass or interface implementation in one expression. Both may capture local variables only when those variables are final or effectively final.

Anonymous classes remain useful when a one-off implementation needs fields, several methods, or special initialization. When a functional interface needs only a short behavior, a lambda is usually clearer.
sections.caption: prefix is captured safely because it is never reassigned.

sections.title: Choosing the smallest honest scope
paragraphs: Nesting is useful when a type serves only its enclosing abstraction. It reduces namespace clutter and can hide implementation details. Excessive nesting, however, makes construction and testing harder. Promote a nested type to a top-level class when it develops an independent responsibility or is reused elsewhere.

terms: Retaining access to a surrounding value from a nested behavior.
A local variable assigned once even without the final keyword.
The outer object associated with a member inner object.
An unnamed, one-use implementation or subclass.
review: Why does a member inner object require an Outer object?
What can a static nested class access directly?
When is an anonymous class more suitable than a lambda?

opening: Exceptions separate a method's normal result from its failure path. They are most useful when a method cannot fulfill its contract and the caller must either recover, translate the problem, or allow it to propagate. Good exception handling preserves context and keeps cleanup reliable.

sections.title: Compile-time, logical, and runtime failures
paragraphs: A compile-time error prevents class files from being produced; examples include malformed syntax, an unknown name, or an incompatible type. A logical error compiles and runs but produces the wrong result because the algorithm or formula is incorrect. A runtime failure occurs while the program is executing; many, but not all, runtime failures are represented by exceptions.

Exception handling addresses exceptional runtime control flow. It cannot repair invalid syntax, and it does not automatically detect an incorrect algorithm. Those problems require compiler feedback, tests, tracing, and debugging.
sections.note: Classify the failure before choosing a remedy: compiler diagnostics, tests and debugging, or exception handling.

sections.title: The exception hierarchy
paragraphs: Throwable has two major branches. Error represents serious JVM or environment failures that applications normally do not recover from. Exception represents conditions application code may handle. Checked exceptions must be caught or declared; RuntimeException and its subclasses are unchecked.

Checked versus unchecked is a compiler rule, not a measure of severity. A checked exception is appropriate when callers can reasonably anticipate and recover from the condition. An unchecked exception commonly reports a violated precondition, invalid state, or programming mistake.
sections.note: Choose an exception type according to the API contract and the caller's recovery options, not simply according to how alarming the failure feels.

sections.title: try, catch, and propagation
paragraphs: A try block contains operations that share a recovery policy. Several catch blocks may follow one try block and are tested from most specific to most general. A nested try statement is legal when an inner operation has a genuinely different recovery boundary, although excessive nesting usually obscures the control flow. If no compatible catch exists, the exception propagates to the caller and the current method ends.
A catch block should add useful context, recover, or translate the exception. Catching Exception and doing nothing destroys evidence and allows the program to continue in an unknown state.
sections.caption: The catch is placed where the program can explain or recover from the domain failure.

sections.title: throw and throws
paragraphs: throw is an executable statement that transfers control by raising one exception object. throws is part of a method declaration and announces checked exceptions that may escape. A custom exception gives a domain failure a precise name and can carry a cause or additional context.
sections.caption: The method rejects invalid state at the boundary where it is first understood.

sections.title: Cleanup and try-with-resources
paragraphs: finally executes after try and catch whether the operation succeeds or fails, apart from abnormal process termination. It is suitable for cleanup but should not return or throw a new unrelated exception that hides the original failure.

For AutoCloseable objects, try-with-resources is safer. Resources declared in the header close automatically in reverse order. If both the body and close operation fail, the close failure is retained as a suppressed exception rather than replacing the primary one.
sections.caption: Wrapping retains the original exception as the cause while adding application context.

terms: A source problem that prevents successful compilation.
A defect that produces an incorrect result despite successful execution.
Passing an uncaught exception up the call stack.
An exception the compiler requires code to catch or declare.
The original failure retained inside a translated exception.
A secondary resource-closing failure preserved by try-with-resources.
review: How do compile-time, logical, and exceptional runtime failures differ?
What is the practical difference between throw and throws?
Why should specific catch blocks precede general ones?
When is a nested try block justified?
What information is lost when a catch block is empty?
Why is try-with-resources preferable to manual closing?

opening: The Collections Framework supplies reusable data structures and algorithms. Begin with the behavioral contract: whether values form a positional sequence, a unique set, or work waiting in a queue. Then choose an implementation according to access, insertion, membership, and traversal needs.

sections.title: Program to collection interfaces
paragraphs: List represents an ordered sequence and permits duplicates. Set represents unique elements. Queue represents elements waiting to be processed, while Deque supports insertion and removal at both ends.
Declaring variables with these interfaces makes intent visible and permits implementation changes without rewriting callers.
sections.caption: The left-hand type states the contract; the constructor chooses the implementation.

sections.title: Implementation trade-offs
paragraphs: ArrayList provides fast indexed access and efficient appends but may shift elements during insertion. LinkedList links nodes and supports deque operations, yet usually has poorer locality and slow indexed access. HashSet provides average constant-time membership when hashCode and equals are correct.

ArrayDeque is normally the preferred general-purpose stack or queue. PriorityQueue removes the highest-priority element according to its comparator, but iterating over it does not produce globally sorted order.
sections.note: Choose from required semantics and measured behavior. A data structure's name is not a performance guarantee for every workload.

sections.title: Iteration and safe modification
paragraphs: The enhanced for statement is built on Iterable and Iterator. An iterator supplies hasNext(), next(), and sometimes remove(). It separates traversal from the internal representation of the collection.

Structurally modifying most collections while an enhanced-for loop or another iterator is active causes ConcurrentModificationException. Use Iterator.remove(), removeIf(), or collect the desired result into another collection.
sections.caption: Modification occurs through the iterator that controls the traversal.

sections.title: Create, add, find, remove, and traverse
paragraphs: Students should practise the same operation vocabulary across collection types. Lists use positional access and preserve duplicates; sets use membership; queues expose the head through peek and remove it through poll.

A failed duplicate insertion into a set is normal information, not an exception. Queue operations such as offer, peek, and poll provide non-throwing forms that are convenient when emptiness is expected.
sections.caption: The method names reflect each interface's contract.

sections.title: Implementing Iterable and Iterator
paragraphs: Iterable<T> belongs to the container. Its iterator() method creates an Iterator<T> that owns one traversal cursor. The iterator answers whether an element remains and returns the next element. Returning a fresh iterator allows two loops to traverse the same container independently.

A custom iterator should throw NoSuchElementException when next() is called after exhaustion. The enhanced for statement obtains an iterator automatically, which is why implementing Iterable makes a custom type usable in for-each.
sections.caption: Iterable supplies the traversal factory; each Iterator represents one traversal.

terms: An object that groups and manages values.
A positional sequence that permits duplicates.
A collection organized around elements waiting to be processed.
An object that advances through elements without exposing representation.
Best-effort detection of unsupported structural modification during iteration.
review: Which interface best expresses a unique collection of values?
When is ArrayDeque preferable to LinkedList?
Does iterating a PriorityQueue return sorted order?
Why should removal during traversal use the active Iterator?
What responsibilities belong to Iterable and Iterator?

opening: Ordering and key-value lookup add another design layer to the Collections Framework. The program must decide whether order is absent, based on comparison, based on insertion, or updated by access. It must also distinguish general-purpose collection contracts from specialized and legacy utilities.

sections.title: Equality, hashing, and ordering
paragraphs: Hash-based collections use hashCode to choose a bucket and equals to confirm identity. Equal objects must have equal hash codes, and equality fields should not change while the object is stored in a hash structure.

Comparable defines one natural order inside the type. Comparator defines an external or alternate order. Comparison must be antisymmetric and transitive; use Integer.compare, Double.compare, or Comparator factories rather than subtraction.
sections.caption: Student owns its natural ID order; callers can independently request grade order.

sections.title: Sorting arrays and lists
paragraphs: Arrays.sort orders arrays; List.sort and Collections.sort reorder mutable lists. Natural ordering is used when no comparator is supplied. A Comparator provides an alternate rule and can be composed with thenComparing for deterministic tie-breaking.
TreeSet and TreeMap apply comparison as elements or keys enter the structure rather than performing a later one-time sort.
sections.caption: Comparator composition makes the primary rule and tie-breaker visible.

sections.title: Map contracts and traversal
paragraphs: Map associates unique keys with values but does not extend Collection. HashMap provides no iteration-order guarantee. TreeMap sorts keys. LinkedHashMap preserves insertion order by default.
When both key and value are required, traverse entrySet() so each association is represented directly.
sections.caption: An entry represents one key-value association.

sections.title: Insertion order, access order, and bounded caches
paragraphs: LinkedHashMap's three-argument constructor can enable access order, where successful access moves an entry toward the end. Combining access order with removeEldestEntry supports a bounded least-recently-used policy.
Without accessOrder=true, the same removal hook evicts according to insertion order instead. The constructor choice is therefore part of the data structure's behavior.
sections.note: Do not infer an ordering contract from one printed HashMap result; only documented contracts are portable.

sections.title: Specialized and legacy utilities
paragraphs: Properties stores String keys and values and supports configuration load/store formats. BitSet represents non-negative indexes as compact bits and supplies logical set operations.

Hashtable and Enumeration are legacy APIs. StringTokenizer is also a legacy tokenizer. Existing programs may require them, but new designs normally choose HashMap or ConcurrentHashMap, collection views or Iterator, and split, Scanner, or a deliberate parser according to the problem.
sections.note: Recognizing a legacy API does not make it invalid; it means compatibility rather than modern design is usually the reason to retain it.

sections.title: Combining maps with persistent account data
paragraphs: A menu-driven account program uses a Map for direct lookup by account number and serialization for persistence. These responsibilities should remain separate: map operations manage the current in-memory model, while explicit load and save operations handle files.
File errors must be reported rather than hidden, and resources must be closed automatically. The map contract does not guarantee persistence by itself.
sections.caption: The key expresses the lookup rule; persistence is a separate boundary.

terms: The ordering defined by Comparable on the element type.
An external strategy for comparing two values.
The fullness threshold that triggers hash-table resizing.
The sequence in which entries were added.
An order updated when entries are successfully accessed.
An older supported API retained mainly for compatibility.
review: When should Comparator be used instead of Comparable?
Why must equals and hashCode agree?
How do HashMap, TreeMap, and LinkedHashMap differ in ordering?
What changes when LinkedHashMap uses access order?
Which specialized problem is solved by BitSet?
Why should map storage and file persistence be treated as separate responsibilities?

opening: Generics let one algorithm or data structure work with many reference types while preserving compile-time type safety. Instead of storing Object and casting later, code declares a type parameter that the compiler tracks through every operation.

sections.title: Generic classes and methods
paragraphs: A type parameter is a placeholder chosen when the generic type is used. Box<String> and Box<Integer> share one implementation but expose different compile-time APIs. The diamond operator asks the compiler to infer constructor type arguments.
A generic method declares its own type parameter before its return type. Its type parameter is independent of any type parameter declared by the surrounding class.
sections.caption: The compiler knows that first(List<String>) returns String without a cast.

sections.title: Invariance and bounded type parameters
paragraphs: Even though Integer extends Number, List<Integer> is not a subtype of List<Number>. If it were, a caller could add a Double to a list that promises to contain only Integer values. Generic types are therefore invariant by default.

A bounded parameter such as <T extends Number> restricts acceptable types and makes Number operations available inside the implementation. Multiple bounds are written with one class bound first, followed by interface bounds.
sections.caption: The bound states exactly which operations the algorithm requires.

sections.title: Wildcards and PECS
paragraphs: A wildcard describes a family of parameterized types. List<? extends Number> may refer to a list of Integer, Double, or another Number subtype. It is safe to read values as Number, but unsafe to add a specific number. List<? super Integer> accepts Integer values, but values read from it are known only as Object.
The mnemonic PECS means producer extends, consumer super. Use extends when an argument produces T values for the method; use super when the method consumes or inserts T values.
sections.caption: The bounds preserve flexibility without abandoning type safety.

sections.title: Type erasure and restrictions
paragraphs: Java implements most generics through type erasure. Type arguments guide compilation but are usually not reified as distinct runtime classes. Consequently, code cannot directly create new T(), new T[], test instanceof List<String>, or use primitives such as List<int>.
Raw types such as List bypass generic checking for compatibility with older Java code. They should not be used in new code because they move errors from compilation to runtime.

sections.title: Generic inheritance preserves its declared type
paragraphs: A generic class or interface can be extended or implemented just like a non-generic type. ArrayList<E> implements List<E>, and List<E> extends Collection<E>; the same E is carried through the relationship. A specialized subclass may either keep a parameter open or fix it to one concrete type.

This does not make Box<Integer> a subtype of Box<Number>. Those are two parameterizations of the same generic class and remain invariant. When an API needs a family of related parameterizations, bounded wildcards express that relationship.
sections.caption: The first subclass carries T forward; the second fixes the inherited parameter to String.

terms: A declared placeholder such as T used inside generic code.
A concrete type such as String supplied to a generic declaration.
The question-mark form representing an unknown type argument.
The runtime implementation strategy that removes most generic type arguments.
review: Why is List<Integer> not a subtype of List<Number>?
Where is a generic method's type parameter declared?
What does PECS mean?
Why can Java not directly create new T()?

opening: Lambda expressions allow behavior to be passed as data. Streams build on that idea by describing a transformation pipeline—what should be selected, transformed, ordered, and combined—without manually controlling every loop step.

sections.title: Functional interfaces give lambdas a type
paragraphs: A lambda is not an untyped block of code. Its target type must be a functional interface with exactly one abstract method. The interface determines the parameter types, return type, and allowed checked exceptions. Default and static interface methods do not count against the single-abstract-method rule.
sections.caption: Predicate tests, Consumer acts, Function transforms, and Supplier produces.

sections.title: Parameters, capture, and method references
paragraphs: Parameter types may be inferred, parentheses may be omitted for one inferred parameter, and braces may be omitted for one expression. A lambda may capture instance fields and local variables that are final or effectively final. This restriction gives the captured local value stable meaning even after the method returns.
A method reference is a concise lambda when an existing method already has the required shape. Common forms are Class::staticMethod, object::instanceMethod, Class::instanceMethod, and Class::new.
sections.note: Conciseness is useful only while intent remains obvious. Keep a named lambda when its domain meaning matters.

sections.title: A stream is a pipeline, not a container
paragraphs: A stream does not store elements. It connects a source to zero or more intermediate operations and one terminal operation. filter, map, distinct, and sorted are intermediate; collect, reduce, count, forEach, and findFirst are terminal.

Intermediate operations are lazy. They perform no traversal until a terminal operation requests a result. This allows the implementation to combine operations and stop early for short-circuiting terminals.
sections.code:
String first = names.stream()
    .filter(longName)
    .map(String::toUpperCase)
    .sorted()
    .findFirst()
    .orElseGet(fallback);
sections.caption: Read the pipeline from top to bottom as a description of the result.

sections.title: Purity, reuse, and parallelism
paragraphs: A stream is single-use; after a terminal operation, create a new stream for another traversal. Intermediate operations should avoid shared side effects because they make reasoning difficult and may break under parallel execution.

parallelStream() is not an automatic speed switch. Parallel work has coordination costs and requires associative operations, sufficient data, suitable tasks, and measurement. Begin with a correct sequential pipeline and optimize only from evidence.

terms: An interface with one abstract method that can be a lambda target.
Use of surrounding values inside a lambda.
A lazy operation that returns another stream.
An operation that consumes the pipeline and produces a result or effect.
Finishing without processing every source element.
review: What supplies the type of a lambda expression?
Why are stream intermediate operations called lazy?
Can a stream be reused after count() or collect()?
Why can side effects become unsafe in a parallel pipeline?

opening: Reflection lets a running program inspect types, members, and metadata. Annotations attach structured metadata to program elements. Together they enable frameworks, test runners, serializers, and dependency injection—but they should be used deliberately because they move some guarantees from compile time to runtime.

sections.title: Class objects are runtime type descriptions
paragraphs: Every loaded type has a Class object. It can be obtained with MyType.class, object.getClass(), or Class.forName(). Class<?> means a class object for some unknown type; Class<T> preserves the relationship to a known T.

getDeclaredFields() and getDeclaredMethods() return members declared directly by the class, regardless of visibility. getMethods() returns public methods including inherited methods. Code must not depend on the order of these returned arrays.
sections.caption: Reflection describes the program rather than invoking its ordinary API directly.

sections.title: Built-in annotations communicate intent
paragraphs: @Override asks the compiler to verify that a method actually overrides or implements an inherited declaration. @Deprecated marks an API that callers should avoid and may provide migration guidance. @SuppressWarnings narrows a deliberate compiler-warning suppression to a selected declaration.

@FunctionalInterface verifies that an interface remains a valid lambda target. @SafeVarargs may suppress specific heap-pollution warnings only on eligible final, static, private, or constructor declarations whose variable-argument handling is genuinely safe. These annotations are checked or interpreted by tools; they do not replace the language rules they describe.
sections.note: Use the narrowest annotation scope and do not suppress a warning until its cause is understood.

sections.title: Annotations are metadata, not behavior
paragraphs: An annotation type is declared with @interface. Its elements look like parameterless methods and may have default values. Applying an annotation records metadata; nothing happens unless the compiler, a tool, or runtime code reads and acts on it.
@Target limits where the annotation may appear. @Retention chooses whether it exists only in source, in the class file, or at runtime. Reflection can read only annotations retained at runtime.
sections.caption: The meta-annotations make the annotation's lifetime and legal location explicit.

sections.title: Discovering and invoking marked methods
paragraphs: A framework-like program can scan methods, request a particular annotation, validate its values, and invoke the method. Reflective invocation wraps a failure thrown by the target method, so production code must unwrap and report the underlying cause carefully.
sections.caption: The annotation supplies data; the loop supplies the behavior.

sections.title: Trade-offs and boundaries
paragraphs: Reflection reduces direct coupling and supports extensible tools, but names and signatures may fail only at runtime. Private-access overrides weaken encapsulation and may be restricted by Java modules. Reflective code is also harder to navigate and test.

Prefer normal interfaces, constructors, and method calls for application logic. Use reflection at infrastructure boundaries where dynamic discovery provides clear value, then validate early and convert failures into meaningful domain errors.

terms: Structured information that describes another program element.
A standard annotation with compiler, tool, or documentation meaning.

opening: A stored program becomes a process when the operating system runs it. A thread is an independent path of execution inside that process. Before coordinating shared state, students need a clear model of how tasks become threads, how thread states change, and how a program requests cancellation or waits for completion.

sections.title: Multiprogramming, multitasking, and multithreading
paragraphs: Multiprogramming keeps several programs available so that the processor can switch when one cannot continue. Multitasking describes the broader experience of multiple tasks making progress through scheduling. Multithreading applies concurrent execution paths within one process.

A process has its own resource boundary. Threads in that process share objects and class state but have separate call stacks. This distinction explains both the efficiency of communication through shared objects and the need to coordinate access to mutable state.

sections.title: Tasks and threads are different ideas
paragraphs: Extending Thread combines the work with the mechanism that runs it. Implementing Runnable separates the task from its execution and is generally easier to reuse. Calling start() asks the JVM to create a new execution path; calling run() is only an ordinary method call on the current thread.
sections.caption: A useful thread name makes logs and debugger views easier to understand.

sections.title: Lifecycle and scheduling
paragraphs: A Thread begins in NEW, becomes RUNNABLE after start(), may enter BLOCKED, WAITING, or TIMED_WAITING, and ends in TERMINATED. RUNNABLE includes both ready-to-run and currently-running states from the JVM's perspective.

Scheduling order is not guaranteed. Priority and yield are hints, not correctness mechanisms. sleep pauses the current thread until the requested duration elapses unless it is interrupted; scheduling may delay the actual resumption. The method does not release intrinsic locks already held.
sections.note: If a program is correct only when one thread happens to run first, the program is not correctly synchronized.

sections.title: Completion, interruption, and daemon threads
paragraphs: join() waits for another thread to terminate and establishes visibility of its completed work. Interruption is a cooperative cancellation request. Blocking methods often respond by throwing InterruptedException; code should stop, propagate the exception, or restore the interrupted status rather than silently swallowing it.

A daemon thread does not keep the JVM alive after all user threads finish. Set daemon status before start(). Daemons are suitable for background assistance, not for work whose final write or cleanup must be guaranteed.
sections.caption: join defines an explicit completion relationship instead of guessing with sleep.

sections.title: Managing a group of worker threads
paragraphs: A group of threads is often represented by a collection of Thread objects. Create each worker from a reusable task, start every worker, and join every worker before consuming the combined result.
ThreadGroup is a legacy organizational API. Ordinary applications usually use collections and, at a more advanced level, executors. The important objective is explicit creation and completion.
sections.caption: Starting and joining in separate loops lets workers overlap before the main thread waits.

terms: A running program with its own operating-system resource boundary.
One path of execution inside a process.
A reusable task contract whose run method can be executed by a thread.
The runtime and operating-system mechanism that selects runnable work.
A cooperative request for a thread to stop or change course.
A background thread that does not keep the JVM alive by itself.
review: How do a program, process, and thread differ?
Why does calling run() not create a new thread?
Which states may occur between NEW and TERMINATED?
What relationship does join() establish?
How should InterruptedException be handled?
When is a daemon thread inappropriate?

opening: Threads share objects and class state, so an apparently simple operation can become incorrect when several execution paths interleave. Synchronization protects a complete invariant; condition coordination lets threads wait efficiently until shared state permits progress.

sections.title: Race conditions and critical sections
paragraphs: An operation such as value++ is a read-modify-write sequence rather than one indivisible action. Two threads can read the same old value and lose one update.
The critical section is the complete region that reads or changes a shared invariant. Protecting only one statement is insufficient when the rule spans a check followed by an update.
sections.caption: Both write and read use the same Counter monitor, providing mutual exclusion and visibility.

sections.title: One monitor must protect one protocol
paragraphs: synchronized acquires an object's intrinsic monitor. Only code using the same monitor participates in the same mutual-exclusion rule. Locking different objects does not protect shared state.

An ATM check-and-withdraw sequence is one transaction. If checking and withdrawal are synchronized separately, another customer may enter between them. The monitor must cover the complete transaction.
sections.note: State the invariant in one sentence, then verify that every read and write participating in it uses the same lock.

sections.title: wait, notify, and condition loops
paragraphs: wait() releases the current object's monitor and suspends the thread. notify() wakes one waiter; notifyAll() wakes all waiters competing for that monitor. These methods must be called while owning the same monitor.
A waiter tests its condition in a while loop because it may wake spuriously or another thread may consume the condition before the waiter reacquires the monitor.
sections.caption: The condition, shared state, and monitor form one protocol.

sections.title: Producer-consumer communication
paragraphs: A producer waits while the shared slot is full, publishes one value, changes the condition, and signals waiters. A consumer waits while the slot is empty, reads the value, changes the condition, and signals again.
Both methods synchronize on the same shared object. Finite production counts and joins make the demonstration repeatable and prevent worker threads from running forever.
sections.note: Despite the older name inter-process communication in some examples, shared-object wait/notify here coordinates threads inside one process.

sections.title: One-to-many coordination
paragraphs: A teacher-and-students example has one writer and several readers. The writer cannot replace the current note until every registered reader has consumed it. Each reader decrements the remaining-reader count and the final reader signals the writer.
The number of readers must be established safely before publication begins. A condition loop protects both early arrival and later wake-up.
sections.note: notifyAll is appropriate when several distinct waiters may need to re-check their own conditions.

sections.title: Keep critical sections deliberate
paragraphs: Holding a monitor during sleep or slow input/output prevents other threads using that monitor from progressing. A short delay may make classroom serialization visible, but production critical sections should contain only the work needed to preserve the invariant.

Higher-level tools such as BlockingQueue, locks, latches, and executors often express common protocols more safely. Understanding monitors remains essential because those tools solve the same coordination problems at a stronger abstraction level.

terms: A result that depends incorrectly on unpredictable timing.
Code that accesses shared state and must execute under mutual exclusion.
The intrinsic lock and waiting mechanism associated with every object.
The guarantee that one thread observes another thread's writes.
A while loop that re-tests whether a waiting thread may proceed.
A multi-step operation observed as one indivisible change to shared state.

opening: Understanding a definition is different from building a program. Integrated practice asks students to translate written requirements into observable behavior, select suitable Java features, and produce evidence that the result works.
The exercises below are cumulative. They can be completed as separate labs or as stages of one student-registration system. Each stage should compile before the next feature is added.

sections.title: A five-step assignment workflow
paragraphs: First, underline nouns that may become domain types and verbs that may become operations. Second, rewrite each requirement as an acceptance criterion that can be observed in output or a test. Third, build the smallest complete path through the program. Fourth, test normal, boundary, and invalid cases. Finally, refactor names and responsibilities without changing behavior.
Keep a short decision log. For every collection, exception, or abstraction, write one sentence explaining why it fits the requirement. This turns code submission into evidence of understanding.
sections.note: Compile after each type or behavior is added. The first error is much easier to diagnose when only a few lines changed.

sections.title: Lab A — validated student import
paragraphs: Create Student, Course, and Enrollment classes in appropriate packages. Read student records from standard input or a file with Scanner. Validate IDs and numeric values before consuming them, preserve names containing spaces, and throw a meaningful custom exception when a complete record violates a domain rule.
bullets: Use private fields and constructors that establish valid objects.
Override one method and call it through a parent or interface reference.
Demonstrate package access across at least two packages.
sections.deliverable: A multi-file project, sample input file, and output showing one accepted and one rejected record.

sections.title: Lab B — collections and ordering
paragraphs: Store accepted students in a List, use a Set to reject duplicate IDs or names according to a stated rule, place pending enrollments in a Queue, and build a Map index for direct lookup. Implement natural ordering and at least one alternate Comparator.
bullets: Create, add, search, remove, and traverse each selected collection.
Sort once with Collections.sort() and once with an explicit Comparator.
Use Iterator to remove invalid or inactive entries safely.
Explain why each interface and implementation was selected.
sections.deliverable: A runnable registry plus a short table mapping each requirement to its collection.

sections.title: Lab C — generic repository and reports
paragraphs: Define Repository<T> and a memory implementation that carries T through its inheritance relationship. Add a generic search or first-match method. Use bounded wildcards for a report that reads numeric data and a method that inserts default integer values where appropriate.
bullets: Show why Repository<Student> cannot be assigned to Repository<Person>.
Use Predicate, Function, Consumer, and Supplier in meaningful roles.
Build one stream pipeline with filtering, mapping, sorting, and a terminal result.
sections.deliverable: Generic source code and three assertions or printed checks that demonstrate type-safe behavior.

sections.title: Lab D — concurrent booking
paragraphs: Model a ticket counter with limited capacity. Launch a collection of worker threads that attempt bookings concurrently. First observe the failure of an unprotected read-modify-write operation, then protect the invariant so that capacity never becomes negative and no ticket is sold twice.
bullets: Create work with Runnable and start several named Thread objects.
Join all workers before reporting the final state.
Identify the shared state, lock, invariant, and critical section.
sections.deliverable: A finite, repeatable demonstration and a paragraph explaining why the corrected version is safe.

sections.title: Submission evidence and self-review
paragraphs: A strong submission contains source files, concise run instructions, representative input, and captured output. It does not rely on an instructor to guess which class contains main or which working directory is required.
Before submitting, remove generated class files, confirm package paths, run from a clean output directory, and compare the result against every acceptance criterion.
sections.code:
Requirement                         Evidence
----------------------------------  ------------------------------
Invalid grade is rejected           Test with -1 and 101
Duplicate student is not inserted   Set size remains unchanged
Students sort by grade              Expected ID order is printed
Iterator removes inactive records   Before/after counts are shown
All booking workers finish          Every worker is joined
sections.caption: An evidence table makes the relationship between requirements and observed behavior explicit.
